summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the sedimentation dynamics of non-Brownian spheres in a semi-dilute suspension across a range of Reynolds numbers from 0.001 to 2.3. Using particle image velocimetry (PIV), the author measures velocity fluctuations and spatial correlations to determine when inertial forces begin to alter the classic Stokes regime behavior. The research identifies a critical Reynolds number, Rec ≈ 0.05, marking the onset of inertial screening. Above this threshold, the inertial screening length becomes comparable to the Stokes sedimentation length, leading to a significant reduction in both the magnitude and spatial extent of velocity fluctuations. The study successfully connects these experimental observations to a modified Hinch force balance model that incorporates Reynolds number-dependent drag coefficients. The findings confirm that inertial effects reduce the correlation sizes and fluctuation amplitudes, with the drag force correction and the reduction in correlation length being of similar importance in explaining the observed dynamics. The results also reconcile previous conflicting reports by re-evaluating the definition of the Reynolds number used in prior studies.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the sedimentation dynamics of non-Brownian spheres in a semi-dilute suspension across a range of Reynolds numbers from 0.001 to 2.3. Using particle image velocimetry (PIV), the author measures velocity fluctuations and spatial correlations to determine when inertial forces begin to alter the classic Stokes regime behavior. The research identifies a critical Reynolds number, Rec ≈ 0.05, marking the onset of inertial screening. Above this threshold, the inertial screening length becomes comparable to the Stokes sedimentation length, leading to a significant reduction in both the magnitude and spatial extent of velocity fluctuations. The study successfully connects these experimental observations to a modified Hinch force balance model that incorporates Reynolds number-dependent drag coefficients. The findings confirm that inertial effects reduce the correlation sizes and fluctuation amplitudes, with the drag force correction and the reduction in correlation length being of similar importance in explaining the observed dynamics. The results also reconcile previous conflicting reports by re-evaluating the definition of the Reynolds number used in prior studies.

Research Context
Sedimentation of non-Brownian spheres is a fundamental problem in physics. Much focus has been on particles slowly settling in viscous liquids. In the Stokes regime, concentrations display Re-independent large amplitude velocity fluctuations. Experiments and simulations have shown fluctuations display a characteristic spatial size ξ. Sedimentation dynamics at higher speed flows where inertial forces become significant have received much less attention. For an isolated sphere falling at moderate Re, there is a distance beyond which the 1/r Stokes like hydrodynamics are screened. Experiments designed to investigate these changes, however, are greatly lacking. We are aware of only a single experiment... that has examined the fluctuation dynamics of spheres at moderate Re.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to demonstrate how moderate amounts of fluid inertia can affect the settling dynamics of spheres. The onset of inertial corrections occurs when the inertial screening length l = a/Re becomes similar to the Stokes sedimentation length ξ0. For Re > Rec, inertial screening significantly reduces both the magnitude and spatial extent of the particle velocity fluctuations. A modified Hinch force balance model connects the fluctuation magnitudes σV /V to the correlation sizes ξ over the entire range studied. The hypothesis is that when the inertial screening length becomes as small as the Stokes correlation length, fluctuations will show an inertial influence. Brenner proposed a different criterion based solely upon a comparison of the particle diffusion coefficient D and the solution viscosity ν. The results suggest that the models underlying assumption of a random particle density distribution remains valid in the presence of inertia.

Methodological Details
The particles used were monodisperse glass beads of radius a = 137±9 µm. They were dispersed in various mixtures of glycerol and water. The volume fraction is φ = 0.06 for all cases. The sample cell was a rectangular glass tube of dimension 8 × 80×305 mm. The temperature was at the ambient value T = 23±10C. Particle velocities were measured using a particle image velocimetry (PIV) apparatus. A large cross section of the cell was imaged (3×3 cm). Each velocity fields is a map of 41 × 42 vectors. Each velocity vector is the local average of two to four spheres. The Reynolds number range studied is 0.001 ≤Re ≤2.3. The Reynolds number is defined as Re ≡2V a/ν.

Procedures And Architectures
Initially, random dispersions were prepared by vigorous shaking of the cells. The location of the imaging window was far from both the sedimentation front and the sediment growth. Key Results
For Re <∼0.05, ξ is independent of Re as expected in the Stokes regime. The values are all in good agreement with the scaling relation ξ0 ≈11aφ−1/3. For Re >∼0.05, the behavior begins to change, and ξ follows a roughly logarithmic decay with Re. The decrease of ξ with Re demonstrates that inertial screening occurs at shorter distances for higher Reynolds numbers. σV /V is independent of Re for Re <∼0.05, and the value σV /V ≈0.75 is in good agreement with results found in Stokes flow sedimentation. At our highest speed, Re = 2.3, σv/V is reduced by ≈80%. The agreement over the entire range of Reynolds numbers is remarkably good. The drop in fluctuation magnitudes with Re is due to both the decreasing correlation lengths ξ and the increasing drag force term βRe. The critical Reynolds number for the appearance of inertial influence, Rec = a/ξ0, can also be evaluated from their findings resulting in Rec ≈0.06. The region where ν/D ∼1 is indeed where significant deviations to Stokes behavior are seen.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The success of the Hinch model in connecting σV /V with ξ suggests that the models underlying assumption of a random particle density distribution remains valid. These results provide an important benchmark for future theoretical work on moderately inertial systems. The onset of inertial corrections occurs when the inertial screening length l = a/Re becomes as small as the Stokes velocity correlation length ξ0. At higher Reynolds numbers, inertial screening reduces the size and magnitude of the velocity correlations. The results generally confirm the Brenner picture that particle diffusion becomes similar to viscous momentum diffusion.
